title: The rain-cloud of dharma (4.29)
hook: a yogi who wants no interest, even on the highest knowledge, and the cloud that opens
tomorrow: The afflictions end; knowledge becomes infinite (4.30–4.31)

segments.voice: Yesterday, sutras 4.25 and 4.26: nimna. Your line was the mind inclines to freedom, like a marble finding the bottom of a bowl. Did something go easily downhill? Day four hundred eighty-seven.

Every app on your phone wants you to collect something. Points, streaks, badges, miles, a little gold star for the tenth coffee. It works on us because we like to see a return. Even a spiritual practice can quietly turn into that: so much meditation, so much calm, a balance growing in an account somewhere. Patanjali has one word for the person who has stopped keeping that account, even for the highest thing there is. It comes from the world of money. And the sutra it sits in ends with weather.
screen: `POINTS, STREAKS, BADGES, GOLD STARS.` → `A PRACTICE CAN BECOME AN ACCOUNT.` → `A WORD FROM THE WORLD OF MONEY.`

segments.voice: Sutra 4.29: prasankhyane 'py akusidasya sarvatha vivekakhyater dharmameghah samadhih. Even toward the highest discernment, for one who takes no interest, from discernment in every way, comes the samadhi called the cloud of dharma. The money word is kusida. It means lending at interest, or the interest itself. A-kusida is someone who charges none. Who has reached the very top of discernment, the clearest seeing there is, and doesn't try to collect on it. Doesn't want powers from it, doesn't want status, doesn't even want to hold onto it as an achievement. Earlier in the text, Patanjali warned that the powers are obstacles, and that the invitation of the gods should be refused. This is that refusal carried all the way up. And when even that last wanting goes, what arrives is dharma-megha. Megha is a cloud, the heavy rain cloud of the monsoon. Commentators read the image in more than one way. Some hear a cloud that rains dharma, pouring down on everything. Others hear a cloud that rains away every last trace of karma. Either way, it's not a trophy. It's weather. It comes when the sky is ready, and it soaks the whole field. The same name, dharma-megha, also appears in Buddhist texts, for the last stage of the bodhisattva's path. Two neighbors, reaching for the same cloud.
screen: `AKUSIDA: ONE WHO TAKES NO INTEREST.` · `EVEN THE HIGHEST SEEING, NOT COLLECTED.` · `MEGHA: THE MONSOON CLOUD.` · `IT RAINS ON THE WHOLE FIELD.` · then, large: `DHARMAMEGHAḤ SAMĀDHIḤ.`

segments.voice: Sit, and for these two minutes, keep no account. Don't track how calm you are, or how well this is going. If you notice yourself scoring, I'm doing well, I'm doing badly, smile at the scorekeeper and set the pencil down. Just breathe, the way rain falls: not for any reason, not to get anything back. The bell holds the time.
Akusida, one who takes no interest. Dharma-megha samadhi comes to such a person, even at the highest discernment, wanting no return.
Your line: dharma-megha. Today, find one place you're quietly keeping score, a streak, a favor owed, a tally of who called whom, and let that one tally go. Day four hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: In the Yoga tradition, dharma-megha samadhi is described as the last stage before kaivalya, reached only when the practitioner seeks nothing, not even from the highest discernment.

fork.setup: you've reached the clearest discernment there is. what does 4.29 say opens the cloud of dharma?
options: wanting nothing from it at all.
holding it tightly so it stays.
fork.reveal: for one who takes no interest, even in the highest knowledge, comes the samadhi called the cloud of dharma.

original.note: Sanskrit dharma-megha: the cloud of dharma. megha is a rain cloud.

trapdoor: what you thought: the highest stage is the biggest reward.
what it means: it comes when even the highest discernment is wanted for nothing.

what a scholar hears: prasankhyana is the highest reflective knowledge; akusida, from kusida, interest on a loan, is one who seeks no return from it; commentators differ on whether the cloud rains dharma or rains away karma.
